sections.label: Repeal of Sedition Act
sections.summary: This Bill repeals the Sedition Act and makes related amendments to other legislation.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This Bill repeals the Sedition Act and makes related amendments to other legislation.

sections.label: Conduct promoting ill-will between groups
sections.summary: Other laws now cover matters once under the Sedition Act, but conduct promoting ill-will and hostility between groups remains unaddressed.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But over time, as other laws come into place, which were originally covered by the Sedition Act, including: "(a) conduct which impugns the integrity and impartiality of Judges or undermines public confidence in the administration of justice in Singapore", have already been dealt with under the common law of contempt, but now there is the Administration of Justice Act; "(b) inciting violence with the objective of effecting change to policies in Singapore" have now and for some time found a place in other legislation; and "(c) ill-will or hostility between groups of people in Singapore".

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But one aspect, which is not in any other legislation, which remains relevant and has not been dealt with, therefore, is conduct that promotes feelings of ill-will and hostility between different groups in the population, not just along racial or religious lines but other lines as well.

sections.label: Amendment to Penal Code section 267C
sections.summary: The Bill amends section 267C of the Penal Code to cover this.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Bill, therefore, amends section 267C of the Penal Code to cover this.

sections.label: Making offences arrestable under CPC
sections.summary: After repeal, the Criminal Procedure Code is to be amended to make certain offences arrestable so Police investigations on social cohesion remain effective.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Once the Sedition Act is repealed, to ensure that the Police can continue to be effective in investigations where particularly social cohesion is concerned, we propose to amend the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC) to make the following offences arrestable.

sections.label: MHA view on Sedition Act
sections.summary: MHA has said it finds the Sedition Act of limited application and can be repealed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: MHA has said that for this reason, it finds that the Sedition Act is of limited application and can be repealed.

sections.label: MHA press release on arrestable offences
sections.summary: MHA stated the Sedition Act offences are arrestable and the change ensures Police can act swiftly on egregious cases affecting social cohesion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At paragraph 11 of the MHA press release accompanying the First Reading of this Bill, MHA pointed out that the offences under the Sedition Act are arrestable and stated that with its repeal, making this change is "to ensure that the Police can continue to act swiftly and effectively when dealing with egregious cases that affect social cohesion".

sections.label: Sedition Act safeguards versus Penal Code
sections.summary: The Sedition Act contains safeguards and exceptions for legitimate speech that sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code do not appear to contain.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: By way of contrast, even the offences in the colonial-era Sedition Act contains safeguards and exceptions to protect legitimate, non-seditious speech, which these sections of the Penal Code do not appear to contain.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In contrast, sections 298 and 298A of the Penal Code as amended by this Bill do not have such express exceptions or safeguards.

sections.label: Sedition Act exception and arrestability
sections.summary: An exception under the Sedition Act would not exist in the amended Penal Code, and MHA added arrestability so Police can act swiftly on egregious cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: What if someone points out something which they know is prejudicial to the maintenance of harmony between different religious or racial groups and is likely to disturb public tranquility but they are doing so for the purpose of trying to point it out so as to remove it?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This would fall under the exception to section 3(2)(d) of the Sedition Act, which is now to be repealed but with the Sedition Act to be repealed, that would not be an exception in the amended Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: MHA's rationale for adding arrestability to these two offences, aside from merely porting these over from the Sedition Act, is also so as "to ensure that the Police can continue to act swiftly and effectively in dealing with egregious cases that affect social cohesion".

sections.label: Sections amended with MRHA
sections.summary: Sections 298 and 298A of the Criminal Procedure Code were amended when the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act was amended in October 2019.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Section 298 and 298A of the Criminal Procedure Code were amended when the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act was amended back in October 2019.

sections.label: MRHA amendments not in force
sections.summary: The passage asks why the amendments to the MRHA passed by Parliament in 2019 are not yet in force.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: If the amendments to the MRHA passed by Parliament in 2019 are not yet in force, why is this the case?

sections.label: Sedition Act six-month time limit
sections.summary: Under the Sedition Act actions must be brought within six months, while the amended provisions have no time limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Under the Sedition Act, actions have to be brought within six months and there is no time limit under the amended provisions.

sections.label: Sedition Act time limit rationale
sections.summary: Raising discontent or disaffection among citizens is an offence regardless of whether it is against the Government, explaining the six-month time limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If you raise the discontent or disaffection amongst the citizens, it does not matter whether it is against the Government or not, that is also an offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, it is a very extreme legislation and we are doing away with it and you can understand why a time limit of six months has been put.

sections.label: Sedition Act elements done away
sections.summary: Statements, words and document offences are covered, and most key Sedition Act elements are done away with, so the six months' requirement is not ported over.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Specifically, we are covering statements made, words uttered and reproduction sale, offer for sale and importation of documents.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: That is the reason why the six months' requirement under the Sedition Act is not being ported over because, basically, most of the key elements of the Sedition Act, which kept the colonial rule in place, are being done away with.

sections.label: Mental elements in proposed amendments
sections.summary: Section 267(2)(d) requires knowing or having reason to believe an intention, and the proposed amendments set mental elements higher than the Sedition Act requires.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And, likewise, under 267(2)(d), there is also a requirement for knowing or having reason to believe an intention.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: So, the mental elements are set out in the proposed amendments, which are at a higher level than what the Sedition Act requires.

sections.label: Lower thresholds and colonial history
sections.summary: The reason for lower thresholds in section 3(1) is its own history of maintaining colonial rule.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The reason for lower thresholds in section 3(1) is due to its own history of maintaining colonial rule.

sections.label: Prejudice of arrestable offence
sections.summary: A counter question asks what the prejudice is if it is made arrestable, which lets the Police move faster and intervene in serious matters.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think a counter question is: what is the prejudice if it is made arrestable?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It allows the Police to move faster, it allows the Police to intervene and these are serious matters.

sections.label: 2019 amendments and religious organisations
sections.summary: The amendments were passed in 2019, and legislation affecting religious organisations requires disclosures and compliance requirements.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The amendments were passed in 2019 but, normally, with many such legislation, which affect a large group of people on the ground – here, it is all the religious organisations – they have to make disclosures, they have compliance requirements.

sections.label: Bringing amendments into force
sections.summary: Systems need time, and the amendments will be brought into force as soon as all these things are in sync.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: And our systems need a little bit of time.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: We will bring it into force as soon as all these things are in sync.
